question: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and how does it work?
title: XSS Cross-Site Scripting – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)** is an injection attack where an attacker gets **malicious JavaScript to run in another user's browser** by smuggling it through data your app renders without encoding. The three types are **stored** (script saved in your DB, e.g. a comment), **reflected** (script bounced back from a request parameter), and **DOM-based** (client-side JS writes untrusted data into the page). The root cause is **rendering untrusted data as HTML**; the fix is **context-aware output encoding** plus a **Content-Security-Policy**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know XSS runs in the victim's browser (not the server) and can name stored vs reflected vs DOM-based
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing XSS with SQL injection; thinking it only affects the attacker; saying 'validate input' is the complete fix instead of output encoding
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the browser can't tell legitimate script from injected script, so the defense is encoding at the output point in the correct context (HTML, attribute, JS)

sections.title: What XSS Is and Why It's Dangerous
sections.content:
**Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)** is an injection flaw where an attacker injects **client-side script** (usually JavaScript) into a page that other users view. When the victim's browser loads the page, it can't distinguish the attacker's script from the site's own code, so it **runs the malicious script with the site's privileges**.

That means the script can **steal session cookies**, log keystrokes, perform actions as the victim, or rewrite the page to phish credentials. Unlike SQL injection, which targets the server's database, **XSS targets other users' browsers** — the server is just the delivery mechanism.

It's part of **OWASP A03:2021 – Injection**. There are three flavors: **stored** (the script is saved server-side, like in a comment, and served to everyone), **reflected** (the script comes from the request and is echoed straight back), and **DOM-based** (client-side JavaScript inserts untrusted data into the DOM). The root cause is always **untrusted data rendered as HTML without encoding**.

sections.title: How Stored XSS Steals a Session
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Attacker posts a comment
containing script tag] --> B[App saves it
without encoding] B --> C[Victim opens the page] C --> D[Browser renders comment
as real HTML + script] D --> E[Script runs in victim's
browser with site privileges] E --> F[Sends document.cookie
to attacker server] F --> G[Attacker hijacks

sections.title: Vulnerable: untrusted data written as raw HTML
Safe: encode on output (and let the template escape)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing XSS with SQL injection**: XSS runs in the *victim's browser*; SQLi runs in the *database*.
- **Thinking only the attacker is affected**: stored XSS hits every user who views the page.
- **Relying on input validation alone**: encode at **output** in the correct context — the same data is safe in one place and dangerous in another.
- **Using `th:utext` / `innerHTML` with user data**: these render raw HTML and re-open the hole.
- **Forgetting HttpOnly cookies**: marking the session cookie `HttpOnly` stops JavaScript from reading it, limiting cookie theft.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **XSS = attacker's JavaScript running in a victim's browser**, with the site's privileges.
- Three types: **stored**, **reflected**, **DOM-based** — all from rendering untrusted data as HTML.
- It targets **users**, not the server; impact includes **session theft and account takeover**.
- Primary fix is **context-aware output encoding**; templates like Thymeleaf escape by default.
- Add **Content-Security-Policy** and **HttpOnly** cookies as defense in depth.
- Part of **OWASP A03 – Injection**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Cross-Site Scripting, or XSS, is an injection attack where an attacker gets malicious JavaScript to run inside another user's browser. The important thing to understand is that, unlike SQL injection which targets the database on the server, XSS targets your users. The server is really just the delivery mechanism. When the victim's browser loads the page, it can't tell the difference between the site's own JavaScript and the attacker's injected script, so it runs both with the same privileges. That lets the attacker steal session cookies, log keystrokes, act as the victim, or rewrite the page to phish for passwords.

There are three types. Stored XSS is when the script is saved on the server — say in a comment or a profile field — and then served to everyone who views that page, so it's the most dangerous. Reflected XSS is when the script comes in through a request parameter and gets echoed straight back in the response. And DOM-based XSS is purely client-side, where the page's own JavaScript takes untrusted data and writes it into the DOM unsafely.

The root cause in every case is the same: untrusted data is rendered as HTML without being encoded. So the main fix is context-aware output encoding — encoding the data at the point where you write it into the page, so that something like a script tag shows up as harmless text instead of executing. In a Spring app, template engines like Thymeleaf escape output by default, which is why you avoid the raw, unescaped variants. On top of that, I'd add a Content-Security-Policy header and mark session cookies HttpOnly so injected JavaScript can't read them — that's defense in depth.

beats.label: the mechanism
beats.content: An attacker submits malicious JavaScript as content — a comment, username, or profile field. Your server stores it and later sends it to other users as part of a page. Their browser sees it as legitimate script from your domain and executes it.

beats.label: stored vs reflected
beats.content: Stored XSS: the payload sits in your database and hits every user who loads that page. Most dangerous — one submission, unlimited victims. Reflected XSS: the payload travels in a URL parameter, gets reflected back in the response. Requires the victim to click a crafted link. Less persistent but still dangerous for phishing.

beats.label: what the script can do
beats.content: Because the script runs under your site's origin, it has full access: steal session cookies, log keystrokes, make authenticated API calls as the victim, redirect them to a phishing page. The browser trusts it completely because it came from your domain.

beats.label: candidates miss
beats.content: candidates miss: conflating XSS with SQL injection. They're different targets entirely — XSS is about injecting code into browsers, SQL injection is about injecting code into databases. A REST API that only returns JSON is far less exposed to XSS than a server-rendered HTML page.

question: How do you prevent XSS in a Java web application?
title: XSS Cross-Site Scripting – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: Prevent XSS by **encoding output in the right context** rather than trusting input. In a Spring app that means: let **Thymeleaf auto-escape** with `th:text` (avoid `th:utext`), never build HTML by string concatenation, **HTML-encode** any user data you must emit (e.g. OWASP Java Encoder), set a **Content-Security-Policy**, mark session cookies **HttpOnly + Secure**, and for rich-text input, **sanitize with an allowlist library** like OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer. The golden rule: **validate input, but encode on output**.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain context matters (HTML body vs attribute vs JS vs URL) and that for HTML you can't strip, you use an allowlist sanitizer, not a blocklist

sections.title: Encode on Output, in the Right Context
sections.content:
The core principle of XSS prevention is **output encoding**: transform user data so the browser treats it as **text, not markup**, at the exact point you write it into a page. You **validate input** for correctness, but you **encode on output** for safety — the same string is harmless in an HTML body and dangerous inside a `<script>` block, so the encoding must match the **context**.

In a typical Spring Boot app rendering HTML with **Thymeleaf**, `th:text` HTML-escapes automatically, so most XSS is prevented just by not using the raw `th:utext` variant. For data you build in Java, use the **OWASP Java Encoder** (`Encode.forHtml`, `Encode.forJavaScript`, `Encode.forUriComponent`).

For features that must accept **rich HTML** (a WYSIWYG editor), you can't escape everything, so you **sanitize with an allowlist** using the **OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer**, keeping safe tags and stripping scripts. Add a **Content-Security-Policy** and **HttpOnly/Secure** cookies as extra layers.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The core principle for preventing XSS in a Java web app is to encode data on output rather than trying to clean it on input. The reason is subtle but important: the same piece of data is harmless in one place and dangerous in another. A string is fine in an HTML body but dangerous inside a script block or a URL, so you have to encode it for the specific context where it lands. That's why output encoding, done at the point you render the data, is the real defense — and why escaping everything on the way in is the wrong layer, because you don't yet know where it'll be used and you can end up double-encoding and corrupting the data.

In a typical Spring Boot app that renders HTML with Thymeleaf, you actually get most of this for free, because th:text HTML-escapes by default. So the main thing is to avoid the raw, unescaped variant, th:utext, when you're displaying user data. If I'm building HTML in Java directly, I'd use the OWASP Java Encoder, which has context-specific methods like forHtml, forJavaScript, and forUriComponent.

There's one case where escaping isn't enough — when a feature genuinely needs to accept some HTML, like a rich-text editor. There you can't just escape everything, so you sanitize using an allowlist library like the OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer. It keeps safe tags like bold and links and strips out scripts and event handlers. The key is that it's an allowlist, not a blocklist — trying to strip out the word script is trivially bypassed with things like an img tag with an onerror handler. Finally, I'd add a Content-Security-Policy header and mark session cookies HttpOnly and Secure, so even if something slips through, the injected script can't read the cookie. That's defense in depth.

question: What is the difference between input sanitization and output encoding?
title: XSS Cross-Site Scripting – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **Input sanitization** cleans data as it arrives — removing or neutralizing dangerous content (e.g. stripping `<script>` from rich text using an allowlist). **Output encoding** transforms data as it's written into a page so the browser renders it as text, not markup (e.g. `<` becomes `<`). The crucial point: **output encoding is the primary XSS defense** because it's context-aware and applied where the data is actually used; sanitization is a **supplementary** measure for fields that must store HTML.

sections.title: Two Different Layers, One Goal
sections.content:
**Input sanitization** and **output encoding** both fight XSS, but at different points in the data's lifecycle. **Sanitization** happens when data **enters** the system: you inspect it and remove or neutralize anything dangerous — typically by running rich-text HTML through an **allowlist sanitizer** that keeps `<b>`/`<a>` and strips `<script>`/`onerror`.

**Output encoding** happens when data **leaves** the system into a page: you transform characters so the browser treats them as text — `<` becomes `<`, `"` becomes `"`. Because the safe encoding depends on **where** the data lands (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, URL), encoding is **context-aware** and applied at render time.

The interview-critical takeaway: **output encoding is the primary defense.** Sanitization can't anticipate every future output context, and over-aggressive sanitization corrupts legitimate data. Encode everything on output; sanitize only the fields that genuinely must store HTML.

sections.content:
| Aspect | Input Sanitization | Output Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| When | As data enters the system | As data is rendered into a page |
| What it does | Removes/neutralizes dangerous content | Converts chars to safe text (`<` → `<`) |
| Context-aware? | No — done before output context is known | Yes — HTML, attribute, JS, URL differ |
| Stored data | Mutated/cleaned permanently | Original kept; encoded only on display |
| Primary XSS defense? | Supplementary | **Yes — the main defense** |

| Best for | Fields that must store HTML (WYSIWYG) | Every place user data is displayed |

sections.title: Relying on sanitization alone (insufficient)
Encode on output (plus sanitize HTML fields)
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use **output encoding everywhere** user-controlled data is displayed — names, comments, search terms, error messages. It's cheap, automatic in Thymeleaf, and context-aware. Treat it as the default that's always on.

Use **input sanitization** for the narrow case where a field must **store and later render real HTML** — a blog post body or a rich-text comment from a WYSIWYG editor. Here you can't simply escape everything (you'd lose the formatting), so you run it through an **allowlist sanitizer** that permits safe tags and removes scripts and event handlers. Even then, keep output handling careful — sanitization complements encoding, it doesn't replace it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Sanitization = clean on input; encoding = neutralize on output** — different layers.
- **Output encoding is the primary XSS defense** because it's applied in the correct context at render time.
- Encoding is **context-aware**: HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, and URL each need different handling.
- **Sanitization is supplementary**, used for fields that must store HTML (allowlist, not blocklist).
- Don't rely on sanitization alone — one missed context becomes an XSS hole.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Input sanitization and output encoding both fight XSS, but they happen at different points in the data's life, and understanding that difference is the key to the question. Input sanitization happens as data comes into the system — you inspect it and remove or neutralize anything dangerous. The typical example is running rich-text HTML through an allowlist sanitizer that keeps safe tags like bold and links but strips out script tags and event handlers. Output encoding happens at the other end, when the data is written into a page — you convert characters so the browser treats them as text. So a less-than sign becomes its HTML entity, and a script tag shows up as literal text instead of executing.

The most important point for an interview is that output encoding is the primary defense, not sanitization. The reason is context. The safe way to encode data depends entirely on where it lands — an HTML body, an HTML attribute, inside a script block, or in a URL all need different encoding. Output encoding is applied at render time, so it can match that context. Sanitization happens before you know where the data will eventually be used, so it can't be context-aware, and if you sanitize too aggressively you corrupt legitimate data.

So in practice, I encode on output everywhere — and in a Spring app with Thymeleaf, th:text does that automatically. I only reach for sanitization in the narrow case where a field genuinely has to store and re-render real HTML, like a rich-text blog post, where I can't just escape everything without losing the formatting. Even then, sanitization complements encoding rather than replacing it. The short version: validate input, but encode on output, and if you only do one thing, make it the encoding.

question: Can XSS affect a REST API that only returns JSON?
title: XSS Cross-Site Scripting – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: A pure JSON REST API is **much lower risk but not automatically safe**. The danger appears when a response is **interpreted as HTML or script** rather than data — e.g. wrong `Content-Type`, browsers MIME-sniffing a response, or a frontend that injects API data into the DOM with `innerHTML`. Defenses: always return `Content-Type: application/json`, send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and ensure the **client encodes data on output**. The API mostly shifts the XSS responsibility to the consumer.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'JSON APIs can't have XSS, period' without the nuance about MIME sniffing, Content-Type, and client-side rendering
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention nosniff + correct Content-Type, and that the SPA consuming the JSON is where the encoding must happen

sections.title: JSON APIs Lower the Risk, Don't Eliminate It
sections.content:
XSS executes in a **browser rendering context**. A REST API that returns **only JSON** and is consumed by code (not rendered as a page) is at **much lower risk**, because JSON data isn't parsed as HTML. But three gaps keep it from being automatic:

1. **Wrong Content-Type** — if user data is returned as `text/html` (or no type), a browser navigating to that URL may render it as a page, executing embedded markup.
2. **MIME sniffing** — some browsers guess the type from content; a JSON body containing `<script>` could be sniffed as HTML. `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` disables this.
3. **Client-side rendering** — the real risk today: a **single-page app** takes API data and injects it with `innerHTML` or `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, executing any script in the data (DOM-based XSS).

So the API should return correct `Content-Type: application/json` with `nosniff`, and the **consuming frontend must encode on output**. The API largely **shifts XSS responsibility to the client**, but both sides have a part to play.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The nuanced answer is that a REST API returning only JSON is at much lower risk of XSS, but it's not automatically immune. The reason is that XSS only executes in a browser rendering context — when something is parsed as HTML and script. Pure JSON data consumed by code isn't rendered as a page, so on its own it doesn't execute. But there are a few gaps that can bring XSS back.

The first is the Content-Type. If an endpoint returns user-controlled data as text/html, or with no content type at all, and a browser navigates directly to that URL, it can render the response as a page and execute any markup in it. So you always want to return application/json. The second gap is MIME sniffing — some browsers try to guess the content type from the body, so a JSON response containing a script tag could be sniffed as HTML. You disable that by sending the X-Content-Type-Options nosniff header, which Spring Security actually sets by default.

But the biggest real-world risk today is on the client side. A single-page app fetches the JSON and then injects that data into the page using something like innerHTML, or React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML. If the data contains a script or an onerror handler, that's DOM-based XSS, and it executes in the user's browser even though the API itself was fine. So the way I'd put it is: a JSON API mostly shifts the XSS responsibility onto the consumer. The server should return the correct content type with nosniff, and the frontend has to encode data on output — using textContent or its framework's default escaping instead of injecting raw HTML.

beats.content: textContent treats the value as plain text — no HTML parsing, no script execution. innerHTML treats it as HTML markup. For any user-supplied data going into the DOM, textContent is the safe choice. This is a frontend concern, but backend developers should communicate it clearly.

beats.label: production trap
beats.content: production trap: APIs that occasionally return text/html Content-Type by mistake — say for error pages or redirect responses. If a browser hits that endpoint and the response contains user-controlled content, the browser renders it as HTML and XSS is possible. Always set Content-Type explicitly.

question: What is Content Security Policy and how does it mitigate XSS?
title: XSS Cross-Site Scripting – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **Content-Security-Policy (CSP)** is an HTTP response header that tells the browser **which sources of scripts, styles, and other content are allowed** to load and run. It mitigates XSS as a **second line of defense**: even if an attacker injects a `<script>`, a strict CSP (e.g. `script-src 'self'`) blocks inline scripts and scripts from unapproved origins, so the injected code never executes. It doesn't fix the underlying bug — **output encoding still comes first** — but it dramatically limits the damage.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand CSP is a browser-enforced allowlist that contains XSS, not a replacement for encoding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking CSP alone prevents XSS, or that 'unsafe-inline' is fine; not knowing it's enforced by the browser
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that blocking inline scripts is what stops most injected payloads, and that you configure it via Spring Security headers

sections.title: A Browser-Enforced Allowlist for Content
sections.content:
**Content-Security-Policy (CSP)** is a response header that defines an **allowlist of trusted sources** for scripts, styles, images, and more. The **browser enforces it**: anything outside the policy — inline scripts, `eval`, scripts from random domains — is simply **refused**.

Against XSS, CSP is a powerful **second line of defense**. Most XSS payloads rely on **inline script** (`<script>...</script>` or `onerror=`). A policy like `script-src 'self'` blocks inline execution and only allows scripts served from your own origin, so an injected payload **fails to run** even though it reached the page. That turns a working exploit into a blocked, logged event.

The key caveat: CSP **does not fix the bug** — the data is still unencoded. **Output encoding remains the primary defense**; CSP shrinks the blast radius when encoding is missed. Also, adding `'unsafe-inline'` to make a legacy app work **defeats the protection**, so you migrate inline scripts to external files or use **nonces/hashes**.

sections.title: How CSP Contains XSS
sections.content:

rose|unsafe-inline|~Avoid this|re-allows inline script|defeats CSP for XSS|legacy crutch only

sections.title: Configuring CSP in Spring Security
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating CSP as the whole fix**: it's a second layer; **output encoding is primary**.
- **Adding `'unsafe-inline'`**: this re-allows inline scripts and largely defeats CSP's XSS value.
- **Forgetting it's browser-enforced**: old browsers may ignore it, so don't depend on CSP alone.
- **Over-broad policies**: `script-src *` allows everything — be specific (`'self'`, named CDNs).
- **Enforcing blind**: roll out with **report-only** first to catch legitimate scripts you'd otherwise break.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CSP is a response header** defining an allowlist of trusted content sources, **enforced by the browser**.
- It mitigates XSS as a **second line of defense** by blocking inline and unapproved scripts.
- A strict `script-src 'self'` stops most injected payloads from executing.
- **`'unsafe-inline'` defeats the protection**; use **nonces or hashes** for needed inline scripts.
- CSP **complements, never replaces, output encoding** — fix the root cause first.
- Configure it via **Spring Security's `headers().contentSecurityPolicy(...)`**; pilot with report-only.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Content-Security-Policy, or CSP, is an HTTP response header that tells the browser which sources of content — scripts, styles, images, and so on — are allowed to load and run on your page. The important thing is that the browser enforces it: anything outside the policy, like an inline script or a script from a domain you didn't approve, is simply refused.

The way it mitigates XSS is as a second line of defense. Most XSS payloads depend on inline script — either a script tag injected into the page or an event handler like onerror. If you set a strict policy, something like script-src self, the browser will only run scripts served from your own origin and will block inline execution entirely. So even if an attacker manages to inject a script tag because you missed an encoding somewhere, that script just doesn't run. It turns a working exploit into a blocked, and ideally logged, event.

The key caveat I'd stress is that CSP doesn't fix the underlying bug — the data is still going out unencoded. So output encoding is still the primary defense, and CSP is there to shrink the damage when something slips through. A common mistake is adding unsafe-inline to make a legacy app work, because that re-allows inline scripts and basically throws away CSP's XSS protection. The right approach for inline scripts you actually need is to use a nonce or a hash. In a Spring Boot app, you configure all of this through Spring Security's headers configuration, with the contentSecurityPolicy method, and I'd usually roll it out in report-only mode first so I can see what it would block before I actually enforce it.

beats.label: how CSP works
beats.content: CSP is an HTTP response header. The server sends it, the browser enforces it. A directive like script-src 'self' tells the browser: only execute JavaScript hosted on this same origin. Any script from an external domain — including an attacker's payload loading from a remote server — gets blocked before it runs.

beats.label: key directives
beats.content: default-src 'self' covers all resource types unless more specific rules override it. script-src controls JavaScript. object-src 'none' blocks Flash and plugins entirely. These are the three most important ones to set for XSS protection. In Spring Security: .contentSecurityPolicy("default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'").

beats.label: nonce for inline scripts
beats.content: Blocking all inline scripts is ideal for XSS protection, but some apps legitimately need them. A nonce is a random value generated per-request, added to both the CSP header and the inline script tag. The browser allows that specific script. Attackers can't predict the nonce so their injected scripts can't include it.

beats.label: gotcha
beats.content: gotcha: adding 'unsafe-inline' to script-src completely breaks XSS protection from CSP. It was a common workaround for legacy inline scripts — but it allows exactly the type of injection CSP was meant to stop. Use nonce-based CSP instead of unsafe-inline.
